## In the tutorial

Try each task in R before you open the answer. More practice for home is in
the final section of this page,
[Extra practice for home](#i-ep02-home).

Tasks 1 to 4 use the Shark Tank file, and money is measured in thousands of
dollars. Tutorial 1 asked how a single predictor relates to the outcome.
This tutorial asks what changes when several predictors are held fixed at
the same time, when categories enter the model, and when a slope depends on
a group or on the season. First build the data for the analysis, with the
same steps as in Lectures 4 to 6. The code converts the requested amount to
thousands of dollars (`ask_1k`). It keeps the 874 deals for a share of the
company (`deals`) for Task 1. For Tasks 2 to 4 it keeps the 1,434 pitches
with a known team classification (`known_gender`). The 7 pitches with an
unknown team are left out, so that all models of Tasks 2 to 4 use the same
observations. Then it makes all-men teams the reference category of the
team variable, builds the dummy `women` (1 for all-women and mixed teams),
and centres the season at its mean.

```{r}
#| label: iep02-load
sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
sharks$ask_1k <- sharks$ask_amount_usd / 1000
deals <- subset(sharks, deal_on_show == 1 & deal_equity_pct > 0)
known_gender <- subset(sharks, pitcher_gender_group != "unknown")
known_gender$gender <- relevel(factor(known_gender$pitcher_gender_group),
                               ref = "all_men")
known_gender$women <- as.integer(
  known_gender$pitcher_gender_group %in% c("all_women", "mixed")
)
known_gender$season_c <- known_gender$season - mean(known_gender$season)
```

### Task 1: Multiple-regression coefficients (Lecture 4)

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} How much of the company do founders give up
in a deal, once the season and the size of the request are taken into
account? With the 874 deals for a share of the company (`deals`), fit a
regression of the equity agreed in the deal, in percent
(`deal_equity_pct`), on the equity that the founder first offered, in
percent (`equity_offered_pct`), the season (`season`), and the requested
amount in thousands of dollars (`ask_1k`). Then answer these questions.

1. Interpret all three slopes with units and with the predictors that are
   held fixed, in one sentence each.
2. The simple regression of the agreed equity on the equity offered, with
   the same deals, gives a slope of about 1.21. Compare it with the slope
   of the equity offered in your model, and explain in one or two sentences
   why the slope changed.
3. Interpret $R^2$ and adjusted $R^2$ in one sentence each. Then name the
   two models that the overall F-test compares, and state its conclusion
   at the 5% level.
4. Give two reasons why the coefficients cannot be read as causal effects,
   in one sentence each.

Use (copy and paste) this structure:

```text
R code:
Interpretation of the equity-offered slope:
Interpretation of the season slope:
Interpretation of the requested-amount slope:
Change in the equity-offered slope, and why:
R-squared:
Adjusted R-squared:
Overall F-test, the two models it compares, and its conclusion:
Two reasons why the coefficients are not causal effects:
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answer

```{r}
#| label: iep02-base-model
m1 <- lm(
  deal_equity_pct ~ equity_offered_pct + season + ask_1k,
  data = deals
)
summary(m1)
mean(deals$deal_equity_pct)   # benchmark: mean agreed equity
cor(deals$season, deals[, c("equity_offered_pct", "deal_equity_pct")])
```

Filled-in structure:

- R code: see the code above.
- Interpretation of the equity-offered slope: among the 874 deals, at the
  same season and requested amount, a founder who offers one percentage
  point more gives up on average about 1.04 percentage points more in the
  deal.
- Interpretation of the season slope: at the same offer and requested
  amount, one later season is associated with about 0.63 percentage points
  less agreed equity, on average. Over ten seasons this adds up to about
  6.3 points, about a quarter of the mean agreed share of 23.6%.
- Interpretation of the requested-amount slope: at the same offer and
  season, an extra \$1,000 requested is associated with about 0.0051
  percentage points less agreed equity (about 0.51 points per \$100,000),
  on average.
- Change in the equity-offered slope, and why: the slope falls from about
  1.21 to about 1.04. In early seasons founders offered larger shares and
  the sharks also took larger shares (both correlations with the season are
  about $-0.40$), so the simple slope partly picked up this season pattern,
  and holding the season fixed removes that part.
- R-squared: $R^2\approx0.433$, so the three predictors explain about 43%
  of the variation in the agreed equity among these deals.
- Adjusted R-squared: $0.431$, almost the same, because the penalty for
  three predictors is small with 874 deals.
- Overall F-test, the two models it compares, and its conclusion: it
  compares the model with the intercept-only model. It gives
  $F\approx221.1$ on 3 and 870 degrees of freedom, with a p-value below
  0.001, so it rejects the null hypothesis that all three slopes are zero.
- Two reasons why the coefficients are not causal effects: any two of
  these. Only pitches that ended in a deal on air are in the data. The
  quality of the venture is not measured, and it can affect both the share
  that a founder offers and the share that the sharks take. The amounts
  and shares may be measured with error.
:::

### Task 2: Dummy variables and a partial F-test (Lecture 5)

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Do founders in some industries offer a
different share of their company? Use the 1,434 pitches with a known team
classification (`known_gender`). Fit a reduced model of the equity offered
(`equity_offered_pct`) on the season and the requested amount (`ask_1k`).
Fit a complete model that adds the industry of the venture (`industry`, 16
industries), with Food and Beverage, the largest industry, as the reference
category.

1. Say how many dummy coefficients the complete model has, and explain in
   one sentence why.
2. Interpret the coefficient of Technology/Software in one sentence. Judge
   its size in one sentence, as a percent of the mean equity offered in
   these pitches.
3. Test with a partial F-test at the 5% level, with the p-value approach,
   whether all industry coefficients are jointly zero.
4. The t-test of the Technology/Software coefficient and the partial
   F-test lead to different conclusions. Explain in one or two sentences
   how this can happen.

Use (copy and paste) this structure:

```text
R code:
Number of dummy coefficients, and why:
Interpretation of the Technology/Software coefficient:
Size, as a percent of the mean equity offered:
Null hypothesis H0:          and alternative hypothesis H1:
Test statistic formula:
Values in the formula:
Value of the test statistic:
P-value:
Conclusion:
Why the t-test and the F-test can disagree:
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answer

```{r}
#| label: iep02-industry-models
known_gender$industry <- relevel(factor(known_gender$industry),
                                 ref = "Food and Beverage")
reduced <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k,
              data = known_gender)
complete <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k + industry,
               data = known_gender)
summary(complete)
anova(reduced, complete)
mean(known_gender$equity_offered_pct)   # benchmark: mean equity offered
```

Filled-in structure:

- R code: see the code above.
- Number of dummy coefficients, and why: 15, one for each of the 16
  industries except the reference category Food and Beverage.
- Interpretation of the Technology/Software coefficient: at the same
  season and requested amount, Technology/Software pitches are fitted to
  offer about 2.95 percentage points less equity than Food and Beverage
  pitches (p $\approx$ 0.004).
- Size, as a percent of the mean equity offered: 2.95 points is about 22%
  of the mean equity offered of 13.2%, a sizeable difference for a founder.
- Null hypothesis H0: all 15 industry coefficients are zero. Alternative
  hypothesis H1: at least one of them is not zero.
- Test statistic formula:
  $F=\dfrac{(\text{SSE}_R-\text{SSE}_C)/q}{\text{SSE}_C/(n-k_C-1)}$.
- Values in the formula: $\text{SSE}_R=83{,}228$,
  $\text{SSE}_C=81{,}858$, $q=15$, and $n-k_C-1=1{,}434-17-1=1{,}416$.
- Value of the test statistic:
  $F=\dfrac{1{,}370.6/15}{81{,}858/1{,}416}=\dfrac{91.37}{57.81}\approx1.58$.
- P-value: about 0.072.
- Conclusion: since $0.072>0.05$, do not reject $H_0$ at the 5% level. The
  data do not show that the industry terms together improve the model.
  This does not prove that all industries offer the same share.
- Why the t-test and the F-test can disagree: the F-test asks whether the
  15 industry terms together improve the model, while each t-test asks
  about one comparison with Food and Beverage. With 15 separate t-tests at
  the 5% level, one p-value below 0.05 can easily occur by chance even if
  no industry differs, because each test rejects a true null hypothesis in
  about 1 of 20 cases.
:::

### Task 3: Interaction (Lecture 6)

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} With the 1,434 pitches with a known team classification (`known_gender`),
fit a regression of the equity offered (`equity_offered_pct`) on the
centred season `season_c`, the dummy `women` (1 for all-women and mixed
teams), their interaction, and the requested amount (`ask_1k`).

1. Write the fitted line for `women = 0` and for `women = 1` at a requested
   amount of \$100,000. Give both season slopes.
2. Calculate the fitted difference in the equity offered between a team
   with women and an all-men team in Season 4, at the same requested
   amount.
3. Interpret the interaction estimate and its p-value in one or two
   sentences, without claiming too much in either direction.
4. Explain in one or two sentences what centring the season changes and
   what it does not change.

Use (copy and paste) this structure:

```text
R code:
Fitted line for women = 0:
Fitted line for women = 1:
Season slope for all-men teams:
Season slope for teams with women:
Fitted difference in Season 4:
Interpretation of the interaction estimate and its p-value:
What centring changes and what it does not change:
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answer

```{r}
#| label: iep02-interaction
m_interaction <- lm(
  equity_offered_pct ~ season_c * women + ask_1k,
  data = known_gender
)
summary(m_interaction)
mean(known_gender$season)   # average season, used for centring
```

Filled-in structure:

- R code: see the code above.
- Fitted line for women = 0: the intercept at \$100,000 requested is
  $13.625-0.00268\times100\approx13.357$, so the line is
  $13.357-0.799\,\text{season\_c}$.
- Fitted line for women = 1: the intercept is $13.357+0.807=14.164$, so
  the line is $14.164-0.861\,\text{season\_c}$.
- Season slope for all-men teams: about $-0.799$ percentage points per
  season.
- Season slope for teams with women: $-0.7994-0.0615\approx-0.861$
  percentage points per season.
- Fitted difference in Season 4: the average season is about 8.78, so
  Season 4 is $\text{season\_c}=4-8.78=-4.78$. The difference is
  $0.807+(-0.0615)\times(-4.78)\approx1.10$ percentage points, about 8% of
  the mean equity offered of 13.2%.
- Interpretation of the interaction estimate and its p-value: the
  estimated difference in slopes is $-0.061$ percentage points per season,
  with p $\approx$ 0.520, so the model gives no evidence that the season
  trends differ between the two groups. It also does not prove that the
  trends are equal, because the estimate is imprecise.
- What centring changes and what it does not change: centring makes the
  `women` coefficient compare the groups at the average season (about 8.8)
  and not at Season 0, which does not exist. It changes neither the fitted
  values nor the interaction estimate.
:::

### Task 4: Polynomial term (Lecture 6)

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} With the 1,434 pitches with a known team
classification (`known_gender`), fit a linear model of the equity offered
(`equity_offered_pct`) on the season and the requested amount (`ask_1k`),
and a quadratic model that adds the square of the season.

1. Decide with a partial F-test at the 5% level whether the quadratic term
   improves the model.
2. Calculate the fitted change from Season 2 to Season 3 and from Season
   14 to Season 15, at the same requested amount. Say in one sentence what
   the comparison of the two changes shows.
3. Calculate the fitted change from Season 18 to Season 19. Explain in one
   or two sentences why you should not use this number.

Use (copy and paste) this structure:

```text
R code:
Null hypothesis H0:          and alternative hypothesis H1:
Value of the test statistic:
P-value:
Conclusion:
Fitted change from Season 2 to Season 3:
Fitted change from Season 14 to Season 15:
What the comparison shows:
Fitted change from Season 18 to Season 19:
Why not to use this number:
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answer

```{r}
#| label: iep02-polynomial
m_linear <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k, data = known_gender)
m_quadratic <- lm(
  equity_offered_pct ~ season + I(season^2) + ask_1k,
  data = known_gender
)
summary(m_quadratic)
anova(m_linear, m_quadratic)
b <- coef(m_quadratic)
# fitted change from season x to x + 1, for x = 2, 14, and 18
b["season"] + b["I(season^2)"] * (2 * c(2, 14, 18) + 1)
```

Filled-in structure:

- R code: see the code above.
- Null hypothesis H0: the coefficient of the quadratic term is zero.
  Alternative hypothesis H1: it is not zero.
- Value of the test statistic: $F\approx20.0$, on 1 and 1,430 degrees of
  freedom.
- P-value: below 0.001.
- Conclusion: reject $H_0$ at the 5% level. The quadratic term improves the
  model.
- Fitted change from Season 2 to Season 3: with $\hat\beta_1\approx-1.713$
  and $\hat\beta_2\approx0.0509$, the change is
  $\hat\beta_1+\hat\beta_2(2\times2+1)=-1.713+5\times0.0509\approx-1.46$
  percentage points, about 11% of the mean equity offered of 13.2%.
- Fitted change from Season 14 to Season 15:
  $-1.713+29\times0.0509\approx-0.24$ percentage points.
- What the comparison shows: the fitted decline flattens, from about 1.5
  points per season in the early seasons to less than a quarter point per
  season in the late seasons.
- Fitted change from Season 18 to Season 19:
  $-1.713+37\times0.0509\approx+0.17$ percentage points, a rise.
- Why not to use this number: the data contain no season after 16, so
  nothing in the data supports this rise. A quadratic curve always turns
  somewhere, and the rise only follows from that shape.
:::

### The models of Tasks 2 to 4 in one table {#iep02-spec-table}

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Lecture 4 showed how research papers put several models side by side in one
regression table. The table below does this for the models of Tasks 2 to 4.
All columns of such a table must use the same observations. Tasks 2 to 4
all use the 1,434 pitches with a known team classification
(`known_gender`), so their models fit in one table. The code prints the one
model output that the answers above do not show, the reduced model of
Task 2.

```{r}
#| label: iep02-table-models
summary(reduced)
```

Column (1) is the reduced model of Task 2 (`reduced`), column (2) the
complete model of Task 2 (`complete`), column (3) the interaction model of
Task 3 (`m_interaction`), and column (4) the quadratic model of Task 4
(`m_quadratic`).

::: {.reg-table}
| | (1) | (2) | (3) | (4) |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Season | −0.815\*\*\* | −0.819\*\*\* | −0.799\*\*\* | −1.713\*\*\* |
| | (0.047) | (0.048) | (0.066) | (0.206) |
| Season squared | | | | 0.051\*\*\* |
| | | | | (0.011) |
| Amount requested (\$1,000s) | −0.0029\*\*\* | −0.0028\*\*\* | −0.0027\*\*\* | −0.0027\*\*\* |
| | (0.0006) | (0.0006) | (0.0006) | (0.0006) |
| Industry dummies (15) | | Yes | | |
| Team with women (all-women or mixed) | | | 0.807 | |
| | | | (0.412) | |
| Season × team with women | | | −0.061 | |
| | | | (0.096) | |
| Intercept | 21.185\*\*\* | 21.265\*\*\* | 13.625\*\*\* | 24.168\*\*\* |
| | (0.484) | (0.631) | (0.335) | (0.822) |
| Observations | 1,434 | 1,434 | 1,434 | 1,434 |
| $R^2$ | 0.187 | 0.200 | 0.189 | 0.198 |
| Adjusted $R^2$ | 0.186 | 0.191 | 0.187 | 0.197 |
:::

Outcome: equity offered (%). Ordinary least squares. Standard errors in
parentheses. All four columns use the same 1,434 pitches with a known team
classification. In column (2), "Yes" means that the model contains the 15
industry dummies, with Food and Beverage as the reference category. Many
papers report a large set of dummies in this short way. In column (3) the
reference category is all-men teams, and season is centred at its mean
(about 8.8), so the intercept and the coefficient of "Team with women"
refer to the average season.
\* p < 0.05, \*\* p < 0.01, \*\*\* p < 0.001.

Read along the Season row. The coefficient is close to $-0.8$ in
columns (1) to (3). In column (4) it is $-1.713$, because with the quadratic term in
the model the season coefficient alone is not the trend. Read down a column
to see one model. Columns (2), (3), and (4) each add terms to column (1), so
a partial F-test can compare each of them with column (1). The bottom rows
show that the four models fit almost equally well: adjusted $R^2$ lies
between 0.186 and 0.197, a difference of about one percentage point of the
variation in the equity offered. Use this layout for regression results in
your thesis.

### Task 5: Read a regression table from a paper

The table below has the layout of a regression table in a research paper,
the same layout as the table above. The outcome is entrepreneurial
intention on a scale from 1 to 7, measured in a survey of 265 students.
Self-efficacy is a score from 1 to 7 for how confident a student is that he
or she can start a business. The table does not show the intercept. Some
journals do this.

::: {.reg-table}
| | (1) | (2) |
|:---|---:|---:|
| Age (years) | 0.02 | 0.01 |
| | (0.02) | (0.02) |
| Female (1 = yes) | −0.21\* | −0.15 |
| | (0.10) | (0.10) |
| Prior entrepreneurial experience (1 = yes) | | 0.42\*\* |
| | | (0.13) |
| Entrepreneurial self-efficacy (1--7) | | 0.38\*\*\* |
| | | (0.07) |
| Observations | 265 | 265 |
| $R^2$ | 0.03 | 0.19 |
| Adjusted $R^2$ | 0.02 | 0.18 |
:::

Outcome: entrepreneurial intention (scale from 1 to 7). Ordinary least
squares. Standard errors in parentheses.
\* p < 0.05, \*\* p < 0.01, \*\*\* p < 0.001.

1. Say in one sentence each what the numbers in parentheses and the stars
   mean. Then check the stars of the self-efficacy coefficient with its t
   statistic. The critical value is $t_{0.975,\,260}=1.969$.
2. The coefficient of Female changes from $-0.21$ with a star in column (1)
   to $-0.15$ without a star in column (2). Explain in one or two sentences
   why the coefficient changed. Then say in one or two sentences what the
   missing star does and does not mean.
3. $R^2$ rises from 0.03 to 0.19. Say in one sentence what that means, and
   name the test that shows whether the two added predictors are jointly
   significant.

Use (copy and paste) this structure:

```text
Numbers in parentheses:
Stars:
t statistic of self-efficacy, and check of its stars:
What happened to the Female coefficient:
What the missing star does and does not mean:
What the rise in R-squared says:
Test of the two added predictors:
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answer

Filled-in structure:

- Numbers in parentheses: the standard errors of the coefficients.
- Stars: the p-value of the two-sided t-test of each coefficient against
  zero, with more stars for a smaller p-value.
- t statistic of self-efficacy, and check of its stars:
  $t_{obs}=0.38/0.07\approx5.4$. This is far beyond the critical value
  $t_{0.975,\,260}$ = `qt(0.975, 260)` = 1.969, and p is below 0.001, so
  three stars are correct.
- What happened to the Female coefficient: model (2) holds experience and
  self-efficacy fixed as well, so the coefficient now compares women and
  men with the same age, experience, and self-efficacy. Part of the
  difference of 0.21 points in column (1) went together with differences in
  experience and self-efficacy.
- What the missing star does and does not mean: the 95% confidence
  interval around $-0.15$ includes zero. It does not show that the
  difference is zero.
- What the rise in R-squared says: the two added predictors explain a
  further 16 percentage points of the variation in intentions in this
  sample.
- Test of the two added predictors: a partial F-test of the two nested
  models, model (1) against model (2) on the same 265 students. If you have
  the data, `anova()` of the two fitted models gives this test.
:::

### Task 6: A/B test, moderator and mediator (Lectures 5 and 6)

&#40;a) An online shop for refurbished phones shows 120 new visitors either
its current product page (`new_page = 0`) or a new page with customer
videos (`new_page = 1`). Chance decides which page each visitor sees, 60
visitors per page. The outcome is the value of the first order in euros.
The code below creates the data.

```{r}
#| label: iep02-ab-test
set.seed(21)
# random assignment: 60 zeros (old page) and 60 ones (new page)
new_page <- sample(rep(c(0, 1), each = 60))
# order values in euros, simulated with a true effect of 3 euros
order_value <- round(40 + 3 * new_page + rnorm(120, mean = 0, sd = 8), 2)
ab_shop <- data.frame(new_page, order_value)
```

Regress `order_value` on the treatment dummy `new_page`. Test in five steps,
with the critical value approach at the 5% level, whether the new page
changes the mean order value. The critical value is
$t_{0.975,\,118}=1.980$.
Explain in one or two sentences why $\hat\beta_1$ estimates the average
treatment effect of the new page. Judge its size as a percent of the mean
order value with the old page. Use (copy and paste) this structure:

```text
R code:
Hypotheses:
Test statistic:
Critical value and rejection region:
Observed value:
Conclusion:
Why the coefficient estimates the average treatment effect:
Size, as a percent of the mean order value with the old page:
```

&#40;b) A meal-kit start-up gives a discount coupon at random to half of its
customers. Customers with the coupon order more meal kits. The coupon raises
orders more for students than for other customers. The coupon also brings
customers to the website more often, and more visits go with more orders.
Which variable is a moderator, and which is a mediator? Say in one or two
sentences each how it appears in a regression of orders on the coupon
dummy. Use (copy and paste) this structure:

```text
Moderator, and how it appears in the regression:
Mediator, and how it appears in the regression:
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answer

&#40;a)

```{r}
#| label: iep02-ab-fit
ab_fit <- lm(order_value ~ new_page, data = ab_shop)
summary(ab_fit)$coefficients
qt(0.975, df = 118)
```

Filled-in structure:

- R code: see the code above.
- Hypotheses: $H_0:\beta_1=0$, the new page has no effect on the mean
  order value. $H_1:\beta_1\ne0$. The significance level is 5%.
- Test statistic: $T=\hat\beta_1/\operatorname{SE}(\hat\beta_1)$, with
  $df=n-k-1=118$.
- Critical value and rejection region: $t_{0.975,\,118}=1.980$. Reject
  $H_0$ if $|t_{obs}|\ge1.980$.
- Observed value: $t_{obs}=3.409/1.341\approx2.54$.
- Conclusion: $2.54\ge1.980$, so reject $H_0$ (p $\approx$ 0.012). At the
  5% level, the new page raises the mean order value.
- Why the coefficient estimates the average treatment effect: chance
  decided who saw the new page, so the two groups are alike on average in
  everything else, measured or not, and the only systematic difference is
  the page.
- Size, as a percent of the mean order value with the old page: the mean
  order value is 39.09 euros with the old page (the intercept) and
  $39.09+3.41=42.50$ euros with the new page. The effect of about 3.41
  euros is about 8.7% of 39.09 euros.

&#40;b)

Filled-in structure:

- Moderator, and how it appears in the regression: student status is the
  moderator, because it changes the slope of the coupon. It enters as an
  interaction, `lm(orders ~ coupon * student)`, and the coefficient of
  `coupon:student` is the difference in the coupon effect between students
  and other customers.
- Mediator, and how it appears in the regression: website visits are the
  mediator, because they lie on the path from the coupon to orders. Adding
  visits, `lm(orders ~ coupon + visits)`, shrinks the coupon coefficient to
  the direct part, so for the total effect of the coupon, leave visits out
  of the model.
:::

### Task 7: Check the AI (Lectures 4 to 6)

Lisa runs a café on campus. On 150 days she recorded the daily sales in
euros, the number of flyers that she handed out that day, the temperature,
and whether the day was in an exam week. The data are observational: Lisa
decided herself on which days she handed out how many flyers. She fitted a
multiple regression and gave its output to an AI assistant:

```text
Outcome: daily sales (€), 150 days       Estimate  Std. Error
Flyers handed out (100s)                     18.0         5.0
Temperature (°C)                              6.5         1.2
Exam week (1 = yes)                         -85.0        22.0
Intercept                                   420.0        35.0
```

The reference category of the dummy is days outside exam weeks. The
critical value for a 95% confidence interval and a 5% test is
$t_{0.975,\,146}=1.976$.

She asked: "Should I hand out more flyers?" The AI answered:

> "Your model controls for the temperature and for exam weeks. So it shows
> the causal effect of flyers: every 100 extra flyers will raise your daily
> sales by €18. In exam weeks, your café sells on average €85 less per day
> than on an average day. The 95% confidence interval of the flyer
> coefficient does not include zero, so the coefficient is significantly
> different from zero at the 5% level."

1. The AI answer contains exactly two errors. Name each error and explain
   it in one sentence.
2. Rewrite the two wrong statements so that the output supports them, in
   one sentence each.

Printing 100 flyers costs €3, and Lisa hands them out herself. Of each euro
of sales, 50 cents are left as margin after the direct costs.

3. Calculate the 95% confidence interval of the flyer coefficient. Then
   calculate the extra daily margin that goes with 100 more flyers, at the
   lower and at the upper end of the interval.
4. Decide whether Lisa should hand out 100 more flyers per day on the basis
   of these numbers, and give your reason in one sentence. Then explain in
   one sentence one reason why her true gain could differ from these
   numbers.

Use (copy and paste) this structure:

```text
First error:
Second error:
Correct sentence about the flyer coefficient:
Correct sentence about the exam-week coefficient:
Interval, calculation:
Interval:
Extra margin at both ends:
Decision and reason:
Why her true gain could differ:
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answer

```{r}
#| label: iep02-ai-check
#| include: false
# Checks the numbers of Task 7.
qt(0.975, 150 - 3 - 1)
ci_flyers <- 18 + c(-1, 1) * qt(0.975, 146) * 5
ci_flyers
0.5 * ci_flyers   # extra margin per day at both ends
```

Filled-in structure:

- First error: the controls hold fixed only the temperature and exam
  weeks, and Lisa chose the flyer days herself, so other things on those
  days, for example an event on campus, can raise sales as well and the
  coefficient is not a causal effect.
- Second error: the exam-week coefficient compares exam-week days with the
  reference category, days outside exam weeks, and not with an average
  day.
- Correct sentence about the flyer coefficient: "On days with the same
  temperature and exam-week status, 100 more flyers go with on average €18
  higher fitted daily sales."
- Correct sentence about the exam-week coefficient: "Days in an exam week
  have on average €85 lower fitted daily sales than days outside exam weeks
  with the same number of flyers and the same temperature."
- Interval, calculation: $18.0\pm1.976\times5.0=18.0\pm9.88$.
- Interval: from €8.12 to €27.88 of daily sales per 100 flyers.
- Extra margin at both ends: at 50 cents per euro,
  $0.5\times\text{€}8.12=\text{€}4.06$ and
  $0.5\times\text{€}27.88=\text{€}13.94$ per day.
- Decision and reason: hand out the extra flyers on this evidence, because
  even at the lower end of the interval the extra margin of €4.06 is above
  the €3 that 100 flyers cost.
- Why her true gain could differ: the coefficient is an association in
  observational data, and if Lisa handed out more flyers on days that were
  busy anyway, the true effect of extra flyers can be smaller.

The third sentence of the AI answer is correct: the interval from €8.12 to
€27.88 does not include zero.
:::
:::

## After class

### Individual practice

[Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Build one model of the equity agreed in the
deal (`deal_equity_pct`) for the deals for a share of the company with a
known team classification. Use the equity offered, the season, the
requested amount in \$1,000s, the presenting team, and one extension that
you can justify: an interaction of the equity offered with the dummy
`women` (1 for all-women and mixed teams), or a quadratic term in season
next to the three team categories (`gender`).

Your answer must include:

1. a precise research question,
2. the code that prepares the data, so that someone else can repeat it,
3. one graph of the data before you fit the model,
4. the R formula and the model summary, and, if you compare several models,
   one regression table in the layout of this tutorial,
5. interpretations of the coefficients with units and reference categories,
6. a t-test of one coefficient and an overall or partial F-test,
7. $R^2$, adjusted $R^2$, and residual diagnostics,
8. one graph of fitted values from the model,
9. a conclusion of 150 words that clearly separates three things: the
   association, its uncertainty, and the reasons why it is not causal.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check a model structure

This model structure covers points 4 to 9.

4. A good solution could fit

   ```r
   known_deals <- subset(known_gender,
                         deal_on_show == 1 & deal_equity_pct > 0)
   m <- lm(
     deal_equity_pct ~ equity_offered_pct * women + season + ask_1k,
     data = known_deals
   )
   ```

   or a model with a quadratic term for season and the team dummies. Keep
   `equity_offered_pct` and `women` in the model next to their interaction
   (the hierarchy principle).
5. Name the reference category. Interpret slopes that combine several
   coefficients, or differences between fitted values.
6. Use `anova()` to compare the model with a nested reduced model.
7. Inspect the residuals, including `rstandard()` and Cook's distance.
8. Plot fitted values only inside the observed range of the predictor on
   the horizontal axis.
9. The conclusion must say that the team categories are broad, that only
   pitches that ended in a deal on air are in the data, and that the results
   therefore do not show a causal effect of gender, of the offer, or of the
   season.
:::

   (`season_c * women + ask_1k`), the season slope for teams with women

4. Centring a predictor changes ..., and it does not change ...

### Make it yours

:::: {.utility-prompt}
<span class="label">Two sentences about your own venture</span>

Think of your own venture, or any business you know well. Describe in two
sentences the full analysis that you would run on its data. First, name the
outcome, two predictors, and one extension (a set of dummies, an
interaction, or a quadratic term) that answers a real question. Second,
say which limit you would mention first in your conclusion: selection,
measurement, or omitted variables. There is no wrong answer.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## See an example, then write your own

Take a student-run venture that sells meal-prep boxes on campus. "Outcome: weekly orders. Predictors: advertising spend and price, plus a dummy for exam weeks and its interaction with advertising spend, because I believe advertising works mainly when students are on campus. The first limit is omitted variables: the weather affects both how many flyers I hand out and how many people are on campus, and nothing in my data measures it."

## Extra practice for home {#i-ep02-home}

This task practises the one-way ANOVA table at home.

### Task 8: A one-way ANOVA (Lecture 5)

The online shop for refurbished phones of Task 6 records the delivery time
in hours of 20 orders for each of three couriers. The code below creates
the data.

```{r}
#| label: iep02-anova
set.seed(7)
courier <- factor(rep(c("cycle", "post", "van"), each = 20))
delivery_hours <- round(c(rnorm(20, 20, 6), rnorm(20, 26, 6),
                          rnorm(20, 22, 6)), 1)
deliveries <- data.frame(courier, delivery_hours)
```

Fit the regression of `delivery_hours` on `courier` and make its ANOVA
table. Say which dummies this regression uses, and say in one sentence
each what its two dummy coefficients mean. Test in five steps, with the
critical value approach at the 5% level, whether the mean delivery time is
the same for the three couriers. The critical value of this F-test is 3.16.
Use (copy and paste) this structure:

```text
R code:
Dummies in the regression:
Meaning of the two dummy coefficients:
Hypotheses:
Test statistic, with both degrees of freedom:
Critical value and rejection region:
Observed value:
Conclusion:
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Check your answer

```{r}
#| label: iep02-courier-fit
courier_fit <- lm(delivery_hours ~ courier, data = deliveries)
coef(courier_fit)
anova(courier_fit)
mean(deliveries$delivery_hours)   # overall mean
qf(0.95, 2, 57)
```

Filled-in structure:

- R code: see the code above.
- Dummies in the regression: `post` and `van`, with `cycle` as the
  reference category.
- Meaning of the two dummy coefficients: the intercept, 22.65 hours, is
  the mean delivery time of the cycle courier. The post courier takes on
  average 3.94 hours longer, and the van courier 0.02 hours less.
- Hypotheses: $H_0:\mu_{\text{cycle}}=\mu_{\text{post}}=\mu_{\text{van}}$.
  $H_1$: at least one mean differs. The significance level is 5%.
- Test statistic, with both degrees of freedom: $F$ = mean square of
  `courier` divided by the mean square of the residuals, with $G-1=2$ and
  $n-G=57$ degrees of freedom.
- Critical value and rejection region: the critical value is 3.16. Reject
  $H_0$ if $F_{obs}\ge3.16$.
- Observed value: $F_{obs}=103.62/35.11\approx2.95$.
- Conclusion: $2.95<3.16$ (p $\approx$ 0.060), so do not reject $H_0$. At
  the 5% level, the data do not show that the mean delivery time differs
  between the couriers. This does not prove that the means are equal. The
  largest difference, 3.95 hours between the post and the van courier, is
  about 16% of the overall mean of 23.96 hours.
:::
